summary: RFCs contain fixed elements such as the title page header, standard boilerplates and copyright statements. This informational RFC describes them and updates them to reflect current practice, to show clearly the source of RFC creation and review. It obsoletes RFC 5741.

eli5.summary: The rules for the cover page and fine print of every RFC, including who made it and how it was reviewed.

questions: what is the status of this memo in an rfc
what is the issn of the rfc series
subtitle: The fixed cover-page header and Status of This Memo text that tell readers which stream an RFC came from and how it was reviewed.

tldr.problem: Readers could confuse RFCs that went through the IETF's review with RFCs that had a very different review and approval process.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC title page header names the originating stream, and the Status of This Memo has three paragraphs that state the status, the review the document received, and where to find updates. The exact wording lives on an IAB web page.
tldr.outcome: This RFC obsoletes RFC 5741 and has itself been updated by RFC 9280 and RFC 9920.

today: RFC 7841 is an Informational RFC published in May 2016 that obsoletes RFC 5741; it has since been updated by RFC 9280 and RFC 9920. The exact boilerplate wording is kept on an IAB web page rather than in the RFC.

sections.title: Why RFCs Carry Boilerplate
sections.content:
RFCs contain fixed elements that exist for historical, practical and legal reasons: the title page header, standard boilerplate text and copyright and IPR statements. As the RFC Series evolved, there was growing concern about labeling each RFC clearly. The main requirement is that RFCs published through the IETF's review process must not be easily confused with RFCs that had a very different review and approval process.

This memo describes the common elements of RFC boilerplate and what each kind of information must contain. It leaves the exact text and layout to a web page maintained by the IAB, so that it is easy to maintain. It obsoletes RFC 5741.
sections.eli5: Some papers look official but were checked very differently. The cover page's fine print makes sure you can tell the difference.

sections.title: RFC Streams and Internet Standards
sections.content:
All Internet Standards-related documents are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs are Internet Standards-related documents. The IETF maintains the Internet Standards Process, which covers Standards Track and BCP RFCs. It also produces non-Standards-Track documents (Informational, Experimental and Historic), and everything in the IETF stream is reviewed by the appropriate IETF bodies.

Documents in other streams are not generally reviewed by the IETF for things such as security, congestion control or inappropriate interaction with deployed protocols. They have also not been approved by the IESG or gone through an IETF-wide last call. The IETF therefore disclaims any knowledge of the fitness of those documents for any purpose.
sections.eli5: Think of a school library. Some books were checked by the teachers and some were donated. The label tells you which kind you are holding.

sections.title: The Title Page Header
sections.content:
The front of an RFC names the authors and affiliations and gives the month and year. The other header elements, historically in a left-hand column, are:

  • Document source: the name of the RFC stream. The old label "Network Working Group" is obsoleted for this purpose. The possible entries are Internet Engineering Task Force, Internet Architecture Board, Internet Research Task Force and Independent Submission.
  • Request for Comments: the number assigned by the RFC Editor on publication.
  • A subseries ID and number, for BCPs and STDs. Several RFCs may share one STD number.
  • An optional relation such as Updates or Obsoletes.
  • Category: one of Standards Track, Best Current Practice, Experimental, Informational or Historic.
sections.eli5: The header is the label on the front of a folder: who made it, its number, and what kind of document it is.

sections.title: The Status of This Memo
sections.content:
This section describes the category of the RFC and includes a statement about the stream-specific review of the material, which clarifies the breadth and depth of review. It has three paragraphs.

Paragraph 1 is a single, clearly standing-out sentence identifying the stream-specific status. Paragraph 2 describes the type of review and exposure the document received, defined per stream under the oversight of the RFC Editor and IAB. Paragraph 3 points to where further information can be found, such as whether the RFC was updated or obsoleted, its origin, errata and how to give feedback.

These paragraphs show only the initial status. A document can later become Historic, which cannot be reflected in the document itself and has to be shown in the information that paragraph 3 refers to.
sections.eli5: The first paragraph says what kind of paper this is, the second says who looked it over, and the third says where to check for news about it.

sections.title: Approved Status Texts
sections.content:
Appendix A holds the initial text for the IAB web page. For the first paragraph, a Standards Track document says "This is an Internet Standards Track document." and a Best Current Practice says "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice." Other categories say the document is not a Standards Track specification and give a reason: informational purposes, the historical record, or examination, experimental implementation and evaluation.

The second paragraph depends on the stream. For example, the Independent Submission text says the RFC Editor chose to publish the document at its discretion and makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment. For non-IETF streams, the memo also adds a pointer to Section 2 of this RFC saying such documents are not candidates for any level of Internet Standard.
sections.eli5: There is a ready-made sentence for each kind of document, so every RFC of the same kind says the same thing in the same way.

sections.title: Other Elements and Editor Duties
sections.content:
RFCs also carry a copyright notice that refers to BCP 78 and an intellectual property statement referring to BCP 78 and BCP 79, and an ISSN (2070-1721) that uniquely identifies the RFC series as a serial publication. The RFC Editor is responsible for positioning and layout of these elements and maintains the RFC Style Guide (RFC 7322).

The security section is brief: misunderstanding the status of a memo could cause interoperability problems, and hence security and stability problems. The RFC Editor is also encouraged to show the stream in indices and interfaces.
sections.eli5: Besides the label, every RFC also has a copyright line and a serial number, a bit like a library book has a barcode.
